title: Is it a real outpost? Two checks, any piece
outcomes: Decides in an unlabeled position whether a named square is an outpost for a named piece
Checks both the supporting pawn and the enemy pawns that could still advance to attack the square
Recognises a position where no outpost exists

steps.text: This lesson builds on **Outposts: a square no pawn can reach**. There you planted a knight. Here you judge, without hints, whether a piece already standing on a square is on a *real* outpost. Two questions decide it: does a pawn of yours defend the square, and could an enemy pawn on a neighbouring file still advance to attack it? Any piece can sit there, not only a knight.

A real outpost needs **both** answers right. A pawn of yours defends the square, and no enemy pawn on a neighbouring file is still able to advance and attack it. *Rule of thumb:* no enemy pawn can attack the piece by simply advancing, so pawns usually cannot drive it away. The test ignores pawn captures that change file, and pieces can still trade it off.

steps.title: One pawn changes the verdict
steps.prompt: Only a black pawn differs between the two positions. Predict for the second, then check.

steps.text: Now without prompts. In the next positions nothing tells you whether an outpost exists. Some positions have none, and that is a fine answer. Name the square, the defending pawn, and the enemy pawns on the neighbouring files before you choose.

steps.prompt: Think about the position with no outpost. Which of the two checks failed there: the supporting pawn or the enemy pawns that could still come? Write which one you looked at first, and whether that order is your habit.

fields.label: Did you check both before answering?
